# Joss Armstrong

> Researcher working across information theory, economics, multi-agent systems, cognition, artificial intelligence and autonomous network management.

Canonical site: https://jossarmstrong.org/

- Research overview: https://jossarmstrong.org/research/

- Public works: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/
- About and identifiers: https://jossarmstrong.org/about/
- Machine-readable works catalogue: https://jossarmstrong.org/data/works.json

## Paper explanations
- TACIT, reputation-weighted O-RAN arbitration: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/tacit/
- ORACLE, verifiable O-RAN arbitration workflows: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/oracle/
- IB, interactive source-side information reduction: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/ib/
- Hierarchical selection, animated one-bit feedback along a selected path: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/hierarchical-selection/
- Allocation and verification, the exact 96-agent feasibility example: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/allocation-verification/
- CAMINO, an animated contextual network assessment: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/camino/
- PECDAFs, a visual comparison before a proposed network change: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/pecdafs/
- Cell similarity, interactive patterns and Pearson correlations: https://jossarmstrong.org/works/cell-similarity/

These author companion pages explain the methods, results and limitations, and link to the public papers. IB, hierarchical selection and allocation/verification are explicitly labelled preprints, with links to the versions explained. Their interactive examples use the public papers' equations and constructions. CAMINO's animation illustrates a reported qualitative scenario, not numerical simulation. Reading the pages does not require JavaScript. ORACLE's reported prototype uses majority selection; its results do not describe a combined TACIT-on-ledger deployment.

Works are ordered by descending year within each publication category. Ties retain the existing order; the list does not imply a within-year chronology.

TACIT, ORACLE, PECDAFs and cell similarity include constructed teaching examples, explicitly distinguished from the papers' empirical data. TACIT uses the paper's exact aggregation and reputation-update rules. ORACLE distinguishes rApp policy voting from validator consensus. PECDAFs illustrates observational cohort comparison, not causal identification. Cell similarity separates Pearson correlation, operating levels and SHAP model explanations; the visual contains no synthetic SHAP results.

- Source identification is not fitness testing (arXiv preprint, BibTeX): https://jossarmstrong.org/works/source-identification/

These pages are author records, not interactive explanations. The three Zenodo pages each host the PDF byte-identical to the Zenodo version they name and state the all-versions DOI and the first-posted date. The arXiv page links the arXiv record and version. All summarise the paper from its own abstract.

## Research structure
A central strand studies task-relative information requirements for coordination: what information a decision requires, what can be discarded, and how those requirements change with finite evidence, hierarchy and recursion. Task-relative information contracts and Task-Sufficient Contraction (TSC) were the culmination of earlier results in allocation/verification and hierarchical component selection. The later Recursive Coordination Information Theory (RCIT) paper named their common framework Coordination Information Theory (CIT) and extended it. RCIT separates the information a current decision needs from the information needed to evaluate the circumstances that decision creates. See https://jossarmstrong.org/research/cit/ The wider portfolio includes related and independently motivated work in mechanism design, economic institutions, cognition, multi-agent systems, autonomous networks, privacy, auditability, resource allocation and distributed AI.

Relationships among works should not be inferred as formal dependence merely because two works share a topic. The site distinguishes motivation, formal dependence, application, empirical evidence, independent development and later conceptual connection.
